schema_notes.is_historical_867: True if the barony name is contemporarily attested as a settlement, fortress, or administrative unit by <= 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: True if the barony name directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Records attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.

b_aqtobe.first_mention_attestation: Officially renamed Aktobe in 1999; originally founded in 1869 as the Imperial Russian military fort of Aktyubinsk.
b_aqtobe.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh aq ('white') + töbe ('hill'), referring to the white chalk/limestone heights on which the 19th-century settlement was built.

current_repo_state.name: Tschalap-Kermân
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Founded in 1869 as the Imperial Russian military fort of Aktyubinsk ("White Hill").

b_orskaya.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Orskaya Fortress in 1743 after the original 1735 fortress of Orenburg at the Or–Ural confluence was relocated downstream.
b_orskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival fortress name derived from the Or River (a left tributary of the Ural River) + -skaya.

b_chalap_kerman.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in standard historical sources and appears to be a CK3/mod-specific Turkicized fortress name.

morphemes.translation: uncertain / diluted milk beverage or synthetic element

b_chalap_kerman.etymology_analysis: Unattested/synthetic Turkicized compound combining chalap with kerman ('fortress'); no documented pre-867 settlement.

b_chubar_KAZ.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern settlement (also known as Chubar Kuduk) in Aktobe Region, Kazakhstan, attested only in modern times.
b_chubar_KAZ.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh şubar ('variegated, mottled') + qudyq ('well'), referring to a steppe well; CK3 uses the Russianized form Chubar.

b_atamansku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Orenburg/Ural Cossack settlement (Atamansky vyselok) established in the 18th–19th centuries.
b_atamansku.etymology_analysis: Russian Cossack settlement name derived from the rank/title ataman ('Cossack leader') + adjectival suffix -sky (garbled as Atamansku in CK3).

current_repo_state.name: Suwundûk
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: *Atamansky* is an **18th–19th c.** Orenburg/Ural Cossack stanitsa name.. Resolved via **Suvunduk** (`b_suvunduk`, the **Suunduk River**, a major left tributary of the Upper Ural/Yaik River). $\rightarrow$ *.

b_suvunduk.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Suunduk (Suvunduk) River, a left tributary of the Ural River.
b_suvunduk.etymology_analysis: Hydronym from Turkic/Bashkir Höyöndök (Kazakh Süyindik, Russianized as Suunduk/Suvunduk), a left tributary of the Ural River.

b_santas.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1737 as Iletsky Gorodok by Yaik Cossacks at the confluence of the Ilek and Ural rivers (localized in CK3 as Ilek; internal key b_santas).
b_santas.etymology_analysis: Localized in-game as Ilek (after the Ilek River, a left tributary of the Ural); internal key b_santas reflects Turkic san-tas ('countless stones').

current_repo_state.name: Ilêch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient nomadic hydronym Ilek (tributary of Yaik). Russian line fortress built 1737.

b_barbastau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Barbastau River, a left tributary of the Ural River in West Kazakhstan.
b_barbastau.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym for a left tributary of the Ural River, incorporating bastau ('spring, river source').

b_kbumak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Bolshoy Kumak (Kumak) River, a left tributary of the Ural River near Orsk.
b_kbumak.etymology_analysis: From Turkic/Kazakh qum ('sand') + aq ('white'), meaning 'white sand'; CK3 key b_kbumak is a typo for Kumak.

current_repo_state.name: Kumâch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kumâch).

b_zhitikara.first_mention_attestation: Granted town status as Dzetygara (Zhitikara) in 1939 (name in local volost use by 1921); originally founded in 1880 as the aul of Konildi.
b_zhitikara.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh jeti/jiti ('seven') + qara ('black'), referring to local dark hills or landmarks; Russianized as Zhitikara.

b_orenburg.first_mention_attestation: Founded at its present site on the Ural River in 1743 by Ivan Neplyuev (the name Orenburg was first used in 1735 at the site of modern Orsk).
b_orenburg.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Russian-German fortress name proposed by Ivan Kirilov in 1734, meaning 'fortress on the Or River'.

current_repo_state.name: Ôr-Flôze
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic title evaluated in 1059 Chancellery audit

b_iletsk.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; founded in the 17th century as a Cossack settlement, fortified in the mid-18th century as Iletskaya Zashchita, and renamed Iletsk in the 19th century.
b_iletsk.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name formed from the Ilek River hydronym + adjectival suffix -sk (later prefixed with Sol- 'salt' in the 20th century).

b_birsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1663 as a Russian fortress on the right bank of the Belaya River (granted town status in 1781).
b_birsk.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name derived from the Bir River (Bashkir Börö, traditionally 'wolf water') + Russian -sk suffix.

current_repo_state.name: Bûr-Agîdel
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Russian fortress of Birsk founded in 1663 (over 16th-c. Arkhangelskoye) on the Belaya River.

b_yeldiatzkaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1736 as Eldyatskaya (Yeldyakskaya) Fortress on the right bank of the Ufa River.
b_yeldiatzkaya.etymology_analysis: Russian 18th-century fortress name derived from the local Bashkir Yeldyak clan/volost + -skaya.

b_prigoro_tabynsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded on 14 July 1736 by order of I. K. Kirilov as Tabynskaya Fortress (Prigorod Tabynsk) at the confluence of the Usolka and Belaya rivers.
b_prigoro_tabynsk.etymology_analysis: From Russian prigorod ('suburb/outpost') + Tabynsk, derived from the Bashkir Tabyn tribal/volost ethnonym.

current_repo_state.name: Tabîn
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Russian Prigorod Tabynsk salt-fortress founded in 1736 by Ivan Kirilov.

b_bielaya.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian name of the Belaya River (Bashkir Aghidhel), a major tributary of the Kama.
b_bielaya.etymology_analysis: Russian hydronym meaning 'White [River]', a calque of the Turkic/Bashkir name Aghidhel (Aq 'white' + Idhel 'Volga/great river').

b_ufa.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1574 as a Russian fortress at the confluence of the Belaya and Ufa rivers by order of Ivan IV (city status in 1586).

morphemes.translation: Ufa River (hydronym; possibly from Iranian ap 'water' or Turkic)

b_ufa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ufa River on which the city sits; linguist Aleksandr Matveyev proposed an Iranian origin from ap ('water'), while Turkic etymologies are also debated.

b_sim.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Sim and granted town status in 1942; originally founded in 1759 as Simsky Zavod around an ironworks on the Sim River.
b_sim.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sim River (a tributary of the Belaya River).

b_bugurslan.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1748 as Buguruslanskaya sloboda by Russian settlers on the Bolshoy Kinel River (town status in 1781).
b_bugurslan.etymology_analysis: From Turkic/Bashkir personal or tribal/river name Bugu-Arslan / Bugha-Arslan ('bull-lion').

current_repo_state.name: Urân-Samâre
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Founded in 1748 as a Russian settlement (sloboda) on the Bolshoy Kinel River.

b_bol_uran.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Bolshoy Uran River, a right tributary of the Samara River in Orenburg Oblast.
b_bol_uran.etymology_analysis: Russian qualifier compound ('Great Uran') combining bolshoy ('big/great') with the Turkic/Bashkir hydronym Uran (Soran).

b_sakmarskoi_gorodok.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1724 (fortified 1725) by Yaik Cossack ataman Vasily Arapov as Sakmarsky Gorodok on the Sakmara River (site first mentioned in 1713).
b_sakmarskoi_gorodok.etymology_analysis: Russian Cossack settlement name meaning 'fortified town on the Sakmara River'.

b_kumertau.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1947 as a Soviet brown-coal mining settlement (town status in 1953).
b_kumertau.etymology_analysis: Soviet-era coined Bashkir name from kümer ('coal') + tau ('mountain'), meaning 'Coal Mountain'.

current_repo_state.name: Bursjân-Îch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Founded in 1947 as a Soviet brown-coal mining settlement ("Coal Mountain").

b_prechistenskaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1742 as Prechistenskaya Fortress on the Sakmara fortified line in Orenburg Governorate.

morphemes.translation: Most Pure (epithet of the Virgin Mary)

b_prechistenskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian Orthodox fortress name dedicated to the Prechistaya Bogoroditsa ('Most Pure Mother of God').

b_salavat.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1948 as a Soviet petrochemical settlement named after Bashkir national hero Salavat Yulaev (town status in 1954).
b_salavat.eponym_details: Named after Salavat Yulaev (1754–1800), Bashkir national hero, poet, and leader in Pugachev's Rebellion.
b_salavat.etymology_analysis: Named in 1948 in honor of the 18th-century Bashkir poet and rebel leader Salavat Yulaev.

current_repo_state.name: Tôratau
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Founded in 1948 as a Soviet petrochemical city named after 18th-c. Bashkir poet and rebel Salavat Yulaev (b. 1754); sub-barony `b_sterlitamak` was founded in 1766.

b_teterpush.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in standard historical sources and appears to be a synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name.
b_teterpush.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical and modern Russian/Bashkir gazetteers; likely a garbled or synthetic CK3 barony key.

b_sterlitamak.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1766 as a salt-loading pier and settlement at the confluence of the Sterlya and Ashkadar/Belaya rivers.
b_sterlitamak.etymology_analysis: Hybrid compound from the Sterlya River + Bashkir tamaq ('mouth of a river'), meaning 'mouth of the Sterlya'.

b_belebey.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1715 as a Chuvash/Bashkir-area settlement in Ufa Province and granted town status in 1781.

morphemes.translation: local toponym or personal name of uncertain origin

b_belebey.etymology_analysis: From Bashkir Bäläbäy (Russianized as Belebey), variously explained as an elevated place or a local Turkic/Chuvash name.

b_achaly.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested as a pre-867 settlement (likely reflects local Turkic *asılı/*achaly toponymy such as Lake Asylykul).
b_achaly.etymology_analysis: Uncertain/unattested CK3 barony name in Bashkiria, possibly linked to Turkic/Bashkir toponyms like Asyly (Asylykul).

b_jalmat.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in historical sources as a pre-867 settlement.
b_jalmat.etymology_analysis: Unattested CK3 barony name in the Kama–Zay region; no documented pre-867 settlement.

current_repo_state.name: Dschalmât
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dschalmât).

b_pascherty.first_mention_attestation: Appears as Pascherti on Gerardus Mercator's 1554 map of Europe (and earlier as Bashkort/Pascherti in 14th-century portolan charts) at the approximate position of Ufa.
b_pascherty.etymology_analysis: Late medieval European cartographic rendering of the ethnonym/choronym Bashkort (Bashkir), marking a settlement near modern Ufa.

b_almetyvesk.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Almetyevsk in 1952 (city status in 1953); originally attested in written records in 1735 as the village of Almetyevo.
b_almetyvesk.eponym_details: Named after the 18th-century Bashkir/Tatar personal name Almet (abbreviated from Al-Muhammad; Mullah Almet of Almetyevo, attested 1735).
b_almetyvesk.etymology_analysis: Russianized possessive settlement name from the personal name Almet (Al-Muhammad) + -yevsk.

b_bugulma.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1736 as a settlement on the Bugulma (Bugulminka) River (town status in 1781).
b_bugulma.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Bugulma (Bugulminka) River hydronym, from Tatar Bögelmä ('twist, river bend').

b_siun.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Syun River, a left-bank tributary of the Belaya River in Bashkortostan and Tatarstan.
b_siun.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for the Syun (Bashkir/Tatar Sön) River, a left tributary of the Belaya River.

b_menzelinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1584–1586 as a Russian streltsy outpost on the Menzelya River (town status in 1781).
b_menzelinsk.etymology_analysis: Russian town name formed from the Menzelya River hydronym + -insk suffix.

b_kumych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Kumysh River, a left tributary of the Chusovaya River in Perm Krai (village of Ust-Kumysh attested from the 16th century).
b_kumych.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for a karstic left tributary of the Chusovaya River in Perm Krai.

b_bisserskaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1736 as Bisertskaya Fortress on the Bisert River in Sverdlovsk Oblast.
b_bisserskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian fortress name derived from the Bisert River hydronym + -skaya.

b_klenovskaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1736 as Klenovskaya Fortress on the Bisert/Siberian route in Sverdlovsk Oblast.
b_klenovskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian fortress name derived from klyon ('maple') + -ovskaya.

b_kirgichanskaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1734 (or 1736) as Kirgishanskaya Fortress on the Kirgishanka River in Sverdlovsk Oblast.
b_kirgichanskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian 18th-century fortress name derived from the local Kirgishanka stream/ethnonym + -skaya.

b_lysva.first_mention_attestation: Officially founded in 1785 with the construction of an iron foundry on the Lysva River (an earlier settlement was known from the mid-17th century).
b_lysva.etymology_analysis: From Komi-Permyak lys ('conifer needle') + va ('water, river'), referring to the Lysva River.

b_kutamych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Kutamysh River, a right tributary of the Sylva River in Perm Krai.
b_kutamych.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of Permic/Finno-Ugric origin for a right tributary of the Sylva River in Perm Krai.

b_serga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Serga River, a right tributary of the Ufa River in Sverdlovsk Oblast.
b_serga.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for a right tributary of the Ufa River in Sverdlovsk Oblast.

b_sylva.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Sylva River, the largest tributary of the Chusovaya River in Sverdlovsk Oblast and Perm Krai.
b_sylva.etymology_analysis: From Komi-Permyak syl ('meltwater') + va ('water, river'), meaning 'meltwater river'.

b_perm.first_mention_attestation: Officially named Perm and granted city status in 1781; founded in 1723 as Yegoshikha Copper Factory at the village of Yegoshikha (first mentioned in 1647).
b_perm.etymology_analysis: From Finnic/Uralic *perämaa ('far-away land', cf. Komi Perym, Veps/Finnish perämaa), applied to the historical Perm region and adopted for the city in 1781.

b_kungur.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1648 on the banks of the Kungurka River (rebuilt as a fortress at Mysovskoye in 1663).

morphemes.translation: Kungurka River (possibly from Turkic üngür 'cave' or qongyr 'dark brown')

b_kungur.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kungurka (Kungur) River, variously linked to Turkic qongyr ('dark/brown') or üngür ('cave').

b_ovinskoi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; minor Russian toponym from ovin ('grain-drying barn') with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_ovinskoi.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name derived from ovin ('threshing/drying barn') + adjectival suffix -skoi.

b_krasnooufimsk.first_mention_attestation: Granted town status as Krasnoufimsk in 1781; originally founded in 1736 as Krasnoufimskaya Fortress on the Ufa River.
b_krasnooufimsk.etymology_analysis: Russian compound from Krasny (Yar) + the Ufa River + -sk, meaning 'Krasny [fortress] on the Ufa'.

b_sebur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sebur (Los munts de Sebur / Sebur) in the 1375 Catalan Atlas (derived from 14th-century Franciscan reports such as Johanca Hungarus, 1320, and cognate with Sibir).
b_sebur.etymology_analysis: 14th-century European cartographic form of Sibir (also linked to the Sabir ethnonym or Mongolic šibir 'marshy forest'), denoting the Cis-Ural/Trans-Ural region.

b_okhansk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1597 CE as the village of Okhannoye (also Okhanskoye / Okhan); granted town status as Okhansk in 1781 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_okhansk.etymology_analysis: Derived from Russian 'okhan'' (a type of fishing net used on the Kama River) with the Russian toponymic suffix '-sk'.

b_aluchi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no confirmed historical settlement in Perm Krai.
b_aluchi.etymology_analysis: Unattested CK3 barony name in the Perm region; no documented historical settlement or pre-867 toponym corresponds to 'Aluchi'.

b_saraninskor.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1758 CE as the Saraninsky ironworks settlement (modern Sarana, Krasnoufimsky District, Sverdlovsk Oblast); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Sarana River (often linked to 'saran', wild lily)
adjectival settlement suffix (garbled in CK3 as '-inskor')

b_saraninskor.etymology_analysis: Garbled CK3 rendering of Russian 'Saraninsky' (Saraninsky Zavod), named after the Sarana River with the Russian '-insk-' adjectival suffix.

b_sakmara.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the summer of 1724 CE by Cossack ataman Vasily Arapov (officially established by Senate resolution in 1725 CE as Sakmarsky Gorodok); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sakmara.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Sakmara River (Bashkir 'Haqmar'), a major right tributary of the Ural River.

b_kaginskoi.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1740 CE (with the Kaginsky ironworks established in 1769 CE by Evdokim Demidov on the Kaga River); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kaginskoi.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Russian adjectival form 'Kaginsky' (Kaginsky Zavod, modern Kaga), from the Kaga River plus the '-insk-' suffix.

b_verkouralsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1734 CE as Verkhneyaitskaya fortress; renamed Verkhneuralskaya in 1775 CE after the Yaik River was renamed the Ural, and granted town status as Verkhneuralsk in 1781 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_verkouralsk.etymology_analysis: Compound Russian toponym meaning 'Upper Ural town', combining directional 'verkhne-' ('upper'), the Ural River, and the '-sk' suffix.

b_yuldybayevo.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the mid-18th century CE by Bashkirs of the Tangaur volost (also recorded as Bakirovo/Gumerovo); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_yuldybayevo.eponym_details: Named after Yuldibay, a Bashkir anthroponym (from Turkic 'yul' = road/way) associated with the mid-18th-century village.
b_yuldybayevo.etymology_analysis: Formed from the Bashkir personal name Yuldibay with the Russian possessive suffix '-evo'.

b_yanokul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no confirmed historical settlement.
b_yanokul.etymology_analysis: Unattested CK3 barony name in Bashkiria; no documented pre-867 or historical settlement matches 'Yanokul' (possibly a garbled or synthetic form).

current_repo_state.name: Insêr
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_inzer.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1890 CE during the construction of the Inzer ironworks (1890-1892 CE) in Beloretsky District, Bashkortostan; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_inzer.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Inzer River (Bashkir 'Inyar'), a tributary of the Sim River.

b_kerken.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no confirmed historical settlement in the Urals.
b_kerken.etymology_analysis: Unattested CK3 barony name; no documented settlement or pre-867 toponym in the Ural region corresponds to 'Kerken'.

b_shimal.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no confirmed historical settlement in the Urals.
b_shimal.etymology_analysis: Unattested CK3 barony name; no documented settlement in Perm or Bashkiria corresponds to 'Shimal'.

b_akchim.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 18th century CE as a village in Krasnovishersky District, Perm Krai; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_akchim.etymology_analysis: Named after the Akchim River, a tributary of the Vishera River in northern Perm Krai.

b_ural.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the name 'Ural' for the mountain range and river (formerly Yaik) appears in post-867 Turkic and Russian sources, and does not denote a pre-867 settlement.
b_ural.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ural Mountains (regional oronym), used in CK3 as a barony/county seat without a corresponding pre-867 settlement.

b_vilva.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1811 CE as the Vsevolodo-Vilvensky ironworks settlement on the Vilva River in Perm Krai; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_vilva.eponym_details: Named after Vsevolod Andreevich Vsevolozhsky (1769–1836), founder of the 1811 ironworks settlement Vsevolodo-Vilvensky (modern Vsevolodo-Vilva).
b_vilva.etymology_analysis: Compound of the founder's given name Vsevolod (Vsevolod Vsevolozhsky, 1769–1836) and the Vilva River (from Komi-Permyak vil' 'new/fresh' + va 'water').

b_solikamsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1430 CE by Vologda merchants (the Kalinnikov brothers) as a salt-mining settlement; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_solikamsk.etymology_analysis: Russian compound meaning 'Salt-on-Kama town', combining 'sol'' ('salt'), the Kama River, and the '-sk' suffix.

b_votkinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1759 CE as an Imperial Russian ironworks on the Votka River; granted town status in 1935 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Votka River (linked to 'Votyak', historical exonym for Udmurts)

b_votkinsk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Votka River with the Russian '-insk' settlement suffix.

current_repo_state.name: Obwe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Founded in 1759 as an Imperial Russian ironworks on the Votka River.

b_nytva.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1623 CE as the village of Nytva on the Nytva River (ironworks built 1756 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_nytva.etymology_analysis: Named after the Nytva River, meaning 'green water' in Komi-Permyak or 'silt water' in Mansi.

b_obva.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Obva River in Perm Krai (modern railway settlement is 20th-century).
b_obva.etymology_analysis: Named after the Obva River, from Komi-Permyak 'ob' ('snow') + 'va' ('water', i.e. 'snowmelt water').

b_krasnokamsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1930 CE as Bumstroy around the Kama paper mill and renamed Krasnokamsk in 1933 CE (town status 1938 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_krasnokamsk.etymology_analysis: Soviet-era Russian compound ('Red Kama town') combining 'krasno-' ('red'), the Kama River, and '-sk'.

b_duvan.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 18th century CE by state peasants from Kungursky Uyezd (exact founding year unrecorded); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_duvan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Duvan tribe of the northeastern Bashkirs; excluded from natural proper names as an ethnonym.

b_parizh.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1842 CE as a Nağaybäk Cossack settlement and named after Paris to commemorate the 1814 Battle of Paris; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_parizh.etymology_analysis: Named in 1842 CE after Paris, France, following Russian military victories in the Napoleonic Wars.

b_karabash.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Karabash and granted town status on June 20, 1933 CE; originally founded in 1822 CE as the Soymanovsky gold-mining settlement near Mount Karabash.
b_karabash.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Karabash, from Turkic/Bashkir 'qara' ('black') + 'bash' ('head/peak').

current_repo_state.name: Mijâs
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Founded in 1822 as a gold- and copper-mining settlement in the Southern Urals.

b_revda.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1734 CE as an ironworks settlement on the Revda River (granted town status in 1935 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_revda.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Revda River, a tributary of the Chusovaya River in Sverdlovsk Oblast.

b_zlatoust.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1754 CE as an ironworks settlement on the Ay River and named after Saint John Chrysostom (Ioann Zlatoust); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_zlatoust.etymology_analysis: Named after Saint John Chrysostom (Church Slavonic 'Zlatoust', 'golden-mouthed', 347-407 CE).

b_uiska.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1742 CE as the Uyskaya Cossack line fortress on the Uy River; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_uiska.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival form ('Uyskaya' / 'Uyskoye') derived from the Uy River with the '-sk-' suffix.

current_repo_state.name: Uî-Flutz
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Russian Uyskaya Cossack line fortress founded in 1742.

b_yumanova.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no confirmed historical settlement.
b_yumanova.etymology_analysis: Unattested CK3 barony name in the Southern Urals; no documented settlement or pre-867 toponym corresponds to 'Yumanova'.

b_satka.first_mention_attestation: Founded on November 19, 1758 CE as an iron-mining factory settlement by Baron Stroganov on the Bolshaya Satka River; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_satka.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Satka (Bolshaya Satka) River in Chelyabinsk Oblast.

b_ust-katav.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1758 CE as an ironworks settlement at the confluence of the Katav and Yuryuzan rivers; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ust-katav.etymology_analysis: Russian locator compound meaning 'mouth of the Katav River', excluded from natural proper names due to the 'ust'-' ('mouth of') qualifier.

b_achichskaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1735 CE as Achitskaya Fortress (reflected in CK3 as 'Achichskaya') on the Achit River in Sverdlovsk Oblast; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_achichskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival form of Achitskaya Fortress (modern Achit), derived from the Achit River with the '-skaya' suffix.

b_arti.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1783 CE when merchant Luginin built a mechanical plant on the Artya River (some local sources date initial land grants to 1756 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_arti.etymology_analysis: Named after the Artya River in southwestern Sverdlovsk Oblast.

b_yamantau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mount Yamantau is the highest peak of the Southern Urals (1,640 m) in Bashkortostan, with no pre-867 settlement.

b_chadrinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1662 CE as Shadrinskaya Sloboda on the Iset River; granted town status in 1712 and 1781 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_chadrinsk.eponym_details: Named after a post-867 Russian settler/founder bearing the nickname Shadra (Shadrinskaya Sloboda, 1662 CE).
b_chadrinsk.etymology_analysis: Russian toponymic formation with the '-insk' town suffix.

current_repo_state.name: Isêt
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1142 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_iset.first_mention_attestation: Originally founded around 1645 CE as Temnovskoye in Sverdlovsk Oblast and renamed Isetskoye in 1962 CE (distinct from Isetskoye in Tyumen Oblast, founded 1650 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_iset.etymology_analysis: Named after the Iset River (a major tributary of the Tobol River); the CK3 barony key 'b_iset' uses the bare hydronym.

b_baklanska.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1680 CE as the village of Baklanskaya in Kargapolsky District, Kurgan Oblast (temporarily called Georgiyevskoye in 1724-1737 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_chelabinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1736 CE as the fortress of Chelyaba by Colonel Alexey Tevkelev on the site of a Bashkir village; granted town status in 1787 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_chelabinsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Bashkir name 'Siläbe' / Russian 'Chelyaba' with the '-insk' town suffix.

current_repo_state.name: Silatsch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Russian fortress of Chelyaba founded in 1736 by Colonel Alexey Tevkelev.

b_troizk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1743 CE as a fortress on the Uy River in Chelyabinsk Oblast; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_silach.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after Lake Silach in northern Chelyabinsk Oblast (modern railway station settlement).
b_silach.etymology_analysis: Named after Lake Silach in northern Chelyabinsk Oblast.

b_yekaterinburg.first_mention_attestation: Founded on November 18, 1723 CE by Vasily Tatishchev and Georg Wilhelm de Gennin and named after Empress Catherine I; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_yekaterinburg.eponym_details: Named after Empress Catherine I of Russia (1684-1727), wife of Peter the Great.
b_yekaterinburg.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Russian-German compound meaning 'Catherine's city', honoring Empress Catherine I.

current_repo_state.name: Tschussowe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Founded in 1723 by Vasily Tatishchev and Georg Wilhelm de Gennin and named after Tsaritsa Catherine I.

b_alapaevsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1639 CE at the confluence of the Neyva and Alapaikha rivers (ironworks built 1704 CE; town status 1781 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_alapaevsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Alapaikha River with the Russian '-evsk' town suffix.

b_irbit.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1631 CE as Irbeyevskaya Sloboda and renamed Irbit in 1662 CE (granted town status in 1775 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_irbit.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Irbit River at its confluence with the Nitsa River.

b_kamychlov.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1668 CE as Kamyshevsky ostrog (known as Kamyshlovskaya sloboda from 1687 CE; town status 1781 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kamychlov.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name derived from the Kamyshlovka River ('kamysh', reeds).

b_glazov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1678 CE household census as the village of Glazova on the Cheptsa River (granted town status in 1780 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_glazov.eponym_details: Named after a post-867 Russian settler or clan bearing the personal nickname Glaz ('eye'), forming the possessive village name Glazova -> Glazov (attested 1678 CE).
b_glazov.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive toponym ('Glazova' -> 'Glazov') from the personal/clan nickname 'Glaz' ('eye').

current_repo_state.name: Tscheptse
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Glazov village attested 1678. Ancient river reach of the Cheptsa.

b_igra.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1615 CE census as a village on the Loza River in Udmurtia; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_igra.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Udmurt clan/vorshud name 'Egra', Russianized as 'Igra'.

b_uva.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1923 CE as a logging settlement on the Uva River in Udmurtia; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_uva.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Uva River in the Udmurt Republic.

b_kargadan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; in-game CK3 name associated in neo-Bulgar/popular literature with the medieval Rozhdestvenskoye Gorodishche (Afkula, 9th-14th c. CE) on the Obva River, which lacks pre-867 documentary attestation.

morphemes.translation: purported medieval town name on the Obva River

b_kargadan.etymology_analysis: Name used in CK3 and popular/neo-Bulgar writings for the medieval Rozhdestvenskoye Gorodishche (Afkula) in Perm Krai.

b_kasib.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1623-1624 CE census as the village of Kasib (with 4 households) on the Lysva River in Solikamsky District, Perm Krai; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kasib.etymology_analysis: Historical village name attested in 1623-1624 CE in Solikamsky District, Perm Krai.

b_koca.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1579 CE as Nyrov Pogost and attested under the name Pogost Kosa in 1647 CE (Komi-Permyak 'Kos') in Perm Krai; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_koca.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kosa River (Komi-Permyak 'Kösva' / 'Kös'), a right tributary of the Kama River.

b_karsovay.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1780 CE (first mentioned in 1780 CE in Vyatka/Udmurt parish records; opened as a parish center in 1841 CE).

morphemes.translation: toponymic element / local stream or clan name

b_karsovay.etymology_analysis: Udmurt toponym Karsovay (Карсовай), containing Udmurt kar ('town, settlement, nest') combined with a local Permic element sovay.

b_kolyn.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Russian chronicles as Khlynov/Vyatka in 1374 CE (with some local traditions citing 1181 CE); known in Tatar/Udmurt sources as Kolyn (Qolın / Kylno).

morphemes.translation: historical Tatar exonym for Khlynov (Vyatka / modern Kirov)

b_kolyn.etymology_analysis: Kolyn (Tatar Qolın, Udmurt Kylno) is the historical Turkic/Permic name for Khlynov (later Vyatka, renamed Kirov in 1934), adapted from the Russian/regional name Khlynov.

current_repo_state.name: Nukrât
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Resolved via verified historical center Nukrât documented in tarraconian_titles_1059.md.

b_nukrat.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1542 CE as Noqrat (Nukrat), the center of the Nukrat Tatars in the Vyatka land.

morphemes.translation: Nukrat (Tatar/Arabic-derived name for the Vyatka/Cheptsa region and Karino settlement)

b_nukrat.etymology_analysis: Noqrat (Nukrat) is the Tatar name for the Cheptsa-Vyatka settlement of Karino and the surrounding Vyatka region, first recorded in 1542 CE.

b_suna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1571 CE (later a monastic estate from 1650 CE, also known as Voznesenskoye).
b_suna.etymology_analysis: Named after the Suna River, a Finno-Ugric/Permic hydronym in Kirov Oblast.

b_arkul.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1903 CE as a river-port backwater settlement (first officially listed in 1912 CE; granted urban-type settlement status in 1932 CE).

morphemes.translation: Udmurt / Ar (ethnonym or local toponymic root)

b_arkul.etymology_analysis: From the Arkul backwater (zaton) on the Vyatka River; likely derived from a Mari/Turkic compound with kul ('ravine, cove, lake') and ar.

b_palniki.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern settlement in Dobryansky District, Perm Krai, established in the 20th century in connection with the Levshino–Kizel railway line.
b_palniki.etymology_analysis: From Russian dialectal palnik ('burnt-over forest clearing for agriculture'), pluralized as Palniki.

b_lolog.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; refers to the Lolog River basin in Perm Krai (first adjacent settlement Kosa attested in 1579 CE).
b_lolog.etymology_analysis: Komi-Permyak hydronym Lolög (Лолӧг), a tributary of the Kosa River in Perm Krai.

b_kai.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1538 CE (or 1558 CE) by the Stroganov brothers as Kaygorod; renamed Kay in 1854 CE.

morphemes.translation: bird, gull, or local Permic toponymic root

b_kai.etymology_analysis: Originally Kaygorod ('Kay-town'), founded in the 16th century in the upper Kama basin; the root Kay is of Komi-Permyak origin.

b_elabuga.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological citadel (Yelabuga Devil's Hillfort) dates to the 11th century CE (traditionally dated 1007 CE); first attested in Russian written documents in the early 17th century (1614–1616 CE as Tryokhsvyatskoye; renamed Yelabuga in 1780 CE).
b_elabuga.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of Tatar Alabuğa, from Volga Bulgar/Turkic ala ('variegated') + buğa ('bull' or topographical prominence).

b_izhevsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1760 CE as an ironworks settlement on the Izh River (granted city status in 1918 CE).
b_izhevsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Izh River (Udmurt Oč) with the Russian settlement suffix -evsk.

b_voloz.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name in Udmurtia (possibly a garbled rendering of Vavozh).

morphemes.translation: unattested CK3 barony placeholder (possibly corrupted Vavozh)

b_voloz.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name in Udmurtia/Volga Bulgaria without a matching historical settlement.

b_mozhga.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1835 CE as a settlement around the Syuginsky glass works; renamed Mozhga and granted town status in 1926 CE.
b_mozhga.etymology_analysis: Named after the Udmurt clan/voršud name Možga (Можга), applied to the town in 1926 CE.

b_kazan.first_mention_attestation: Earliest chronicle mention of Old Kazan (Iske Qazan) in the Rogozhsky Chronicle under 1391 CE; New Kazan founded in 1438 CE by Ulugh Muhammad.
b_kazan.etymology_analysis: From Volga Bulgar/Tatar qazan ('cauldron'), traditionally linked to a legend of a dropped cauldron or the cauldron-like depression at the Kazanka River.

current_repo_state.name: Kaschân
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: While Volga Bulgarian Iske Qazan dates to the 11th–13th c. along the Kazanka River, Kazan only eclipsed Bolghar in the 14th–15th c.

b_kashan_VB.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Volga Bulgarian town existing from the 12th to 15th centuries CE; mentioned in Russian chronicles in the late 14th century (sacked in 1391/1399 CE).
b_kashan_VB.etymology_analysis: Medieval Volga Bulgarian city Qaşan (Кашан) on the right bank of the Kama River, flourishing in the 12th–15th centuries CE.

b_otarka.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; recorded in the 1859 List of Inhabited Localities of Kazan Governorate as the village of Otarka (Pokrovskoye) in Mamadyshsky Uyezd.
b_otarka.etymology_analysis: From Turkic/Tatar otar ('pasture, outlying settlement') with the Russian suffix -ka.

b_mamadych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tatar village named after settler Mamadysh developed in the late 14th–15th centuries and received town status as Mamadysh in 1781 CE (distinct from the 1151 CE Rus chronicle mention of the earlier regional Bulgar stronghold Ak Kirmen / Kermenchuk).
b_mamadych.eponym_details: Named after a post-867 Tatar settler/founder named Mamadysh (Mamadış).
b_mamadych.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Tatar personal name Mamadysh (Mamadış), the traditional first settler of the village.

b_arsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Russian chronicles in 1296 CE (also 1379/1380 CE as the Arsk Land, and 1469 CE as a town/fortress).
b_arsk.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation (with -sk suffix) of Tatar Arça, derived from the ethnonym Ar (the Turkic name for the Udmurt population of the region).

b_mari-turek.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1719 CE as Cheremissky Turek (Mari-Turek) on the Turek River.
b_mari-turek.etymology_analysis: Compound of the ethnonym Mari (distinguishing it from Russian Turek) and the Turek River.

b_volzhsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1931 CE as the workers' settlement of Lopatino; renamed Volzhsk and granted town status on July 6, 1940 CE.
b_volzhsk.etymology_analysis: Soviet-era name (1940 CE) derived from the Volga River with the Russian town suffix -sk.

b_yoshkar-ola.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1584 CE as the Russian fortress Tsarevokokshaysk (renamed Krasnokokshaysk in 1919 CE, and Yoshkar-Ola in 1928 CE).
b_yoshkar-ola.etymology_analysis: Meadow Mari compound meaning 'Red City', adopted in 1928 CE to replace Krasnokokshaysk (originally Tsarevokokshaysk, 1584 CE).

b_arda.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; rural selo in Kilemarsky District, Mari El (also called Tserkysola in Hill Mari), attested in modern Russian/Mari administrative records.
b_arda.etymology_analysis: Named after the Arda River (Meadow Mari Arde) in Mari El.

b_tsarevokokchaisk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1584 CE as the Russian military fortress Tsarev Gorod na Kokshage (Tsarevokokshaysk), renamed Krasnokokshaysk in 1919 CE and Yoshkar-Ola in 1928 CE.
b_tsarevokokchaisk.etymology_analysis: Russian compound meaning 'Tsar's town on the Kokshaga (River)', founded in 1584 CE.

b_cykma.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1583 CE by Tsar Ivan IV as Kozmodemyansk; known in Hill Mari as Tsikmä (Cykma).

morphemes.translation: palisade, stockade, fortress (from Russian tyn/chastokol or Turkic)

b_cykma.etymology_analysis: Hill Mari name Tsikmä (Цикмӓ, CK3 Cykma) for the 1583 CE fortress of Kozmodemyansk.

current_repo_state.name: Zîkme
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Zîkme).

b_semenov.first_mention_attestation: First documented mention in 1644 CE as Semyonov's hamlet (later Semyonovo village; town status from 1779 CE).
b_semenov.eponym_details: Named after a post-867 settler named Semyon (first recorded in 1644 CE as Semyonov's hamlet).
b_semenov.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive form from the personal name Semyon ('Semyon's [hamlet]').

b_luch.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern Russian settlement name (e.g. Luch in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast) or synthetic CK3 barony.
b_luch.etymology_analysis: From Russian luch ('ray, beam'), a modern settlement name or synthetic CK3 barony.

b_urzen.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Russian fortress in 1584 CE (Mari tribal town mentioned in the 16th century; CK3 'Urzen' is a variant/corruption of Urzhum).
b_urzen.etymology_analysis: CK3 form Urzen corresponding to Urzhum (Mari Üržüm / Vürzym), a 16th-century Mari town and 1584 CE Russian fortress.

b_vetluga.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1636 CE on the Vetluga River (granted town status in 1778 CE).
b_vetluga.etymology_analysis: Named after the Vetluga River (Mari Vütla), a Finno-Ugric hydronym.

b_vokhma.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1626 CE (also cited as first mentioned in 1658 CE as Voznesenye-Vokhma) in Kostroma Oblast.
b_vokhma.etymology_analysis: Named after the Vokhma River, a Finno-Ugric hydronym in Kostroma Oblast.

b_ashli.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological site dates from the 11th century CE; first mentioned in written sources under 1220 CE in the Tver Chronicle (as Oshel/Ashli, burned by Sviatoslav III of Vladimir).

morphemes.translation: Ashli (possibly from the Esegel/Eskil tribe or grain/provisions)

b_ashli.etymology_analysis: Medieval Volga Bulgarian town Aşlı (Russian chronicles: Oshel), possibly linked to the Bulgar Esegel/Askil tribe.

b_simbirsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1648 CE as the Russian fortress of Simbirsk by boyar Bogdan Khitrovo (renamed Ulyanovsk in 1924 CE; medieval Sinbir hillfort attested in 1603 CE land books).
b_simbirsk.etymology_analysis: Russian fortress name Simbirsk (with -sk suffix) derived from the nearby medieval Sinbir/Simbir settlement.

b_banja.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name in Volga Bulgaria.

morphemes.translation: unattested CK3 barony name (resembling Slavic banya 'bathhouse')

b_banja.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or unattested CK3 barony in c_ashli without a documented medieval settlement in Volga Bulgaria.

b_bolghar.first_mention_attestation: Established in the 10th century CE as the capital of Volga Bulgaria; first attested in written sources by Ahmad ibn Fadlan in 922 CE.
b_bolghar.etymology_analysis: Named after the Volga Bulgar ethnonym (Bolğar), serving as the capital of Volga Bulgaria from the 10th century CE.

b_bilyar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 10th century CE by the Bilär tribe of Volga Bulgars; attested in 12th-century Russian chronicles (as Veliky Gorod, e.g. 1164 CE) and sacked by Mongols in 1236 CE.

morphemes.translation: Bilyar (tribal name of the Volga Bulgars)

b_bilyar.etymology_analysis: Named after the indigenous Bilär tribe of the Volga Bulgars.

b_cukataw.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological layers date to the 10th–13th centuries CE; first attested in Russian chronicles under 1360/1361 CE (as Zhukotin raided by Novgorod ushkuyniks).
b_cukataw.etymology_analysis: Tatar/Bulgar compound Cükätaw (Җүкәтау, Russian Zhukotin), meaning 'Linden Mountain' or 'Steep Mountain'.

b_suvar.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Volga Bulgarian city attested in 10th-century Arabic sources (Ibn Fadlan 922 CE, al-Balkhi) and by coins minted in Suvar starting in 948–949 CE.
b_suvar.etymology_analysis: Named after the Suvar (Suar) tribe of Volga Bulgaria.

b_karabolam.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1367 CE on the Pizzigani brothers' Venetian portolan chart as 'carabolam' in the Middle Volga/Volga Bulgaria region.
b_karabolam.etymology_analysis: Recorded on the 1367 CE Pizzigani portolan chart as carabolam, a medieval Golden Horde/Volga Bulgarian settlement.

b_aqsubay.first_mention_attestation: Settled in the late 17th century CE; first attested in written sources in 1771 CE.
b_aqsubay.eponym_details: Named after Akspay (Aksubay), a post-867 Chuvash/Tatar founder of the settlement.
b_aqsubay.etymology_analysis: From the personal name Akspay / Aksubay (Tatar Aqsubay), Russified as Aksubayevo.

b_elmet.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Almetyevsk in 1952 CE (town status 1953 CE); originally attested on June 24, 1735 CE in a letter by Mullah Almet (Älmät) as the village of Almetyevo.
b_elmet.eponym_details: Named after Mullah Almet (Älmät), a post-867 Bashkir/Tatar figure attested in 1735 CE.
b_elmet.etymology_analysis: From the Bashkir/Tatar personal name Almet (Älmät), Russified as Almetyevo and later Almetyevsk (1953 CE).

b_samar_VB.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1586 CE as a Russian fortress at the confluence of the Volga and Samara rivers (Ibn Fadlan passed through the river confluence area in 921–922 CE).
b_samar_VB.etymology_analysis: Named after the Samara River (possibly from Turkic/Bulgar samar 'bowl, basin' or Indo-Iranian hydronym).

b_pokhnishne.first_mention_attestation: Founded on September 8, 1888 CE as a railway station on the Samara–Ufa railway line (granted town status in 1947 CE).
b_pokhnishne.eponym_details: Named after the post-867 Russian noble Pokhvistnev family (landowners at the 1888 CE railway station).
b_pokhnishne.etymology_analysis: CK3 'Pokhnishne' corresponds to Pokhvistnevo, named after the Russian noble family Pokhvistnev in 1888 CE.

b_neftegorsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1960 CE as an oil-extracting settlement in Samara Oblast (granted town status in 1989 CE).
b_neftegorsk.etymology_analysis: Soviet-era Russian compound meaning 'Oil Town' (founded 1960 CE).

b_buzuluk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1736 CE as the Russian fortress of Buzulukskaya at the confluence of the Samara and Buzuluk rivers (town status in 1781 CE).
b_buzuluk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Buzuluk River (Tatar Bozawlıq, Bashkir Bıźawlıq).

b_yar_calli.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally dated to c. 1172 CE as a Volga Bulgarian settlement (first documented Russian settlement Berezhnye Chelny founded in 1626 CE; Tatar name Yar Çallı).
b_yar_calli.etymology_analysis: Tatar Yar Çallı ('Shore Chelny', translated into Russian as Naberezhnye Chelny).

b_agidel.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1980 CE as a settlement for the construction of the Bashkir Nuclear Power Plant (granted town status in 1991 CE).
b_agidel.etymology_analysis: Named after the Belaya River, known in Bashkir as Ağidel ('White River').

b_tukhchi.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Volga Bulgarian town mentioned in 12th–13th century Russian chronicles (e.g. 1220 CE).
b_tukhchi.etymology_analysis: Medieval Volga Bulgarian town Tuxçın (Тухчин), recorded in Russian chronicles of the 12th–13th centuries CE.
